#131901. Judge blocks FCC early-renewal process for Disney-owned ABC stations, for now

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (406 w)

Judge blocks FCC early-renewal process for Disney-owned ABC stations, for now

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (406 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A judge has temporarily blocked the Federal Communications Commission from continuing its early renewal of a set of broadcast station licenses for Disney-owned ABC.
  • It has been revealed that judge Loren L.
  • In a recent development, "This is not a close case," wrote the federal judge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A judge has temporarily blocked the Federal Communications Commission from continuing its early renewal of a set of broadcast station licenses for Disney-owned ABC.

It has been revealed that judge Loren L. AliKhan of U.S. District Court in Washington granted Disney the preliminary injunction it sought and denied the FCC's attempt to dismiss the suit.

In a recent development, "This is not a close case," wrote the federal judge. "Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face—loss of their broadcast licenses—the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness.".

Recent findings suggest that the broadcast network had filed the lawsuit and followed the FCC beginning its early review of the ABC licenses. The government agency cited concerns around ABC's diversity, equity and inclusion efforts as the reason behind the start of the early renewal — years ahead of their scheduled expiration.

"Today's decision is an notable victory for the First Amendment," noted an ABC spokesperson.

An FCC spokesperson mentioned in a statement that the part of the decision granting ABC's motion "is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law," the Associated Press reported.

In her ruling, AliKhan said that early license renewal proceedings came over a year into the FCC's enforcement push against ABC, starting with an investigation into Disney's employment practices in March 2025 and leading to the renewal proceedings in April this year.

ABC on Tuesday had remarked that it continued to "face irreparable harm" from the administration, which "has been acting" through the FCC, which is run by President Donald Trump appointee Brendan Carr.

AliKhan, a Joe Biden appointee, noted in her ruling that ABC had to change how it handled guest appearances for top demonstrates "The View" and "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" with no candidate for public office appearing on the former and a senatorial candidate's appearance on the latter uploaded to YouTube instead of being broadcast.

"The prospect of license non-renewal has also factored into plaintiffs' calculus of when and how they cover President Trump and political topics," said the judge.

ABC had alleged that Trump and Carr have been making comments "intended to chill their protected speech," and that such comments have escalated since the 2024 presidential election.

The White House and the FCC didn't immediately respond to requests for comment from CNBC.

— CNBC's Dan Mangan contributed to the story.

    #131897. How Trump’s latest tariff moves hand India an edge over rival Asian exporters

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (467 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    How Trump’s latest tariff moves hand India an edge over rival Asian exporters

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (467 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • tariff rates announced Wednesday have signaled that Washington is willing to offer India an edge over its competitors if Latest Delhi agrees to finalize a long-pending trade deal.
    • Recent findings suggest that the Office of the United States Trade Representative has proposed a tariff of 17% on Indian exports if Newly introduced Delhi "were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade" with Washington.
    • Meanwhile, the USTR has proposed tariffs of 18% on Bangladesh, Cambodia, Thailand, and 20% on China and Vietnam, subject to their respective trade deals, handing India a competitive advantage over rival exporters.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The latest U.S. tariff rates announced Wednesday have signaled that Washington is willing to offer India an edge over its competitors if Latest Delhi agrees to finalize a long-pending trade deal.

    Recent findings suggest that the Office of the United States Trade Representative has proposed a tariff of 17% on Indian exports if Newly introduced Delhi "were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade" with Washington. It added that without a trade deal, India could face tariffs of up to 25% under Section 301 investigations encompassing excess production capacity that harms U.S. interests.

    Meanwhile, the USTR has proposed tariffs of 18% on Bangladesh, Cambodia, Thailand, and 20% on China and Vietnam, subject to their respective trade deals, handing India a competitive advantage over rival exporters.

    It has been revealed that the U.S. expects the announcement of a lower tariff rate will encourage Fresh Delhi to sign off on a trade deal before the G20, Atman Trivedi, partner at Washington-based DGA Albright Stonebridge Group, told CNBC.

    India has got a "better bargain with Washington than its main competitors," and it may be enough for the Indian government "to declare victory and secure domestic backing for the deal," Trivedi mentioned.

    In February, U.S. President Donald Trump had declared a deal with India, claiming that Upcoming Delhi had accepted to "Buy American" at a much higher level after the U.S. agreed to slash tariffs to 18% from 50% earlier.

    The India-U.S. trade deal has been pending with both sides indicating there was little room to grant concessions, while the Supreme Court annulling Trump tariffs allowed New Delhi to demand preferential tariffs that give it an edge over competitors.

    "Today's announcement increases the urgency of reaching an agreement," Ronak D. Desai, visiting fellow at Hoover Institution, Stanford University, told CNBC. He added that while the prospect of a 17% tariff may strengthen the economic case for the deal, the threat of a 25% tariff could stir the sensitivity of the Indian government.

    "The Modi government will be particularly sensitive to any perception that India is conceding under American Pressure," Desai remarked.

    India's commerce ministry on Wednesday mentioned it "does not have structural excess capacity in any sector," denying the findings of the USTR investigation, but added that it remains committed to "working closely with the United States towards the early conclusion of the India-U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement.".

    Industry observers note that despite India facing steep tariffs, which were raised to 50%, New Delhi's trade surplus with the U.S. rose to $57.3 billion in 2025 from $45.2 billion in 2024.

    Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Trump are likely to meet in December for the G20 leaders' meeting in Florida, and several experts believe the two leaders could seal the trade deal on the sidelines of the summit.

    #131893. Vance says he was assured Jensen Huang was not under DOJ investigation

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (677 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Vance says he was assured Jensen Huang was not under DOJ investigation

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that Attorney General Todd Blanche told him Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not under investigation.
    • Industry observers note that "I was told by the Department of Justice and multiple officials in our national security apparatus that he was under no investigation," Vance told reporters in Ohio on Wednesday after being asked what assurances he had gotten that Huang was not under investigation.
    • Vance spoke two days after President Donald Trump told CNBC in an interview that an investigation had been done.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that Attorney General Todd Blanche told him Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not under investigation.

    Industry observers note that "I was told by the Department of Justice and multiple officials in our national security apparatus that he was under no investigation," Vance told reporters in Ohio on Wednesday after being asked what assurances he had gotten that Huang was not under investigation. "Not even that he was about to be prosecuted; that he's under no investigation.".

    Vance spoke two days after President Donald Trump told CNBC in an interview that an investigation had been done.

    In a recent development, trump was asked what Blanche had told him about potential criminal liability for Huang and the question of whether Nvidia chips had ended up in China in violation of U.S. export laws.

    "They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he, himself, was exonerated," Trump said Monday.

    Reuters reported Wednesday that the Department of Justice did not conduct a formal investigation into Huang before Trump pushed for his reinstatement as CEO.

    Blanche had concluded there was no evidence Huang had broken any laws based on investigations into Nvidia clients Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed, according to the report.

    The DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Reuters report. And the White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Vance saying Huang was under no investigation when Trump had said there was one. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment about Vance's remarks.

    Blanche on Tuesday dodged questions about whether there had been an investigation.

    "What the president mentioned is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him," Blanche said after being asked whether the DOJ had investigated Huang and, if so, what were the results of the probe.

    Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, after the chipmaker's board of directors noted it had received "input from senior levels of the United States government" that Huang was not a national security risk. Trump took credit for Huang's reinstatement in the interview with CNBC shortly after Nvidia's announcement.

    Huang resigned following The Latest York Times reporting multiple affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing and who was an executive for the Singapore-based cloud provider Megaspeed.

    The reporting added fuel to allegations that Nvidia should have known its artificial intelligence chips were being diverted to China and being used by Chinese companies, violating U.S. export laws.

    In a recent development, "The product they create is a very notable part of us staying ahead of the SI arms race with China. We really do care about ensuring those chips do not fall into the wrong hands," Vance stated, using the Trump administration's preferred acronym for AI, which the president calls "super intelligence.".

    "We actually see this is an opportunity for Nvidia to focus on complying with American export controls, and we think Jensen Huang is going to take that very seriously," Vance continued.

    "We received the assurances that he was not under any significant — he was under no investigation — and the accusations against him were based on anonymous reporting, not on actual evidence," Vance said.

    On Tuesday, Trump left the door open to pardon Huang in an interview with the New York Post, but Vance mentioned on Wednesday that the CEO doesn't need one.

    "I don't think he needs a pardon at all," Vance stated. "I haven't seen any evidence again that he committed a crime. And if there is evidence that he committed a crime, then that's up to relevant authorities to actually bring a prosecution against him.".

    Huang is scheduled to appear for a closed-door interview with House committees about his dealings with Megaspeed on Tuesday. At the same time, Nvidia will hold its annual conference where it showcases new technology in Washington.

    — Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

    Tech Report: ‘Ready for any storm’: UAE minister optimistic on economy as IMF lifts forecast

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The UAE is "very optimistic" about achieving 7%-8% growth next year, the country's economy and tourism minister Abdulla bin Touq Al Marri told CNBC after the latest data from the International Monetary Fund showed the country would avoid a recession in 2026.
    • The IMF last week revised the UAE's real GDP forecast to 0.2% growth in 2026 from a 3.9% contraction predicted a month ago.
    • Sources indicate that he said the tourism industry was already picking up with occupancy rates returning to "almost near normal" and international carriers including British Airways and Air France rerouting flights to the UAE.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The UAE is "very optimistic" about achieving 7%-8% growth next year, the country's economy and tourism minister Abdulla bin Touq Al Marri told CNBC after the latest data from the International Monetary Fund showed the country would avoid a recession in 2026.

    The IMF last week revised the UAE's real GDP forecast to 0.2% growth in 2026 from a 3.9% contraction predicted a month ago. "The UAE is coming back, and that adjustment within one month demonstrates that there is a huge potential aspect when it comes towards the end of the year," the minister told CNBC's Dan Murphy.

    Sources indicate that he said the tourism industry was already picking up with occupancy rates returning to "almost near normal" and international carriers including British Airways and Air France rerouting flights to the UAE. The minister expects economic growth to be higher than 0.2% this year.

    The Iran war has disrupted economic activity in the UAE, with missile and drone attacks from Tehran and maritime disruptions weighing on energy trade, tourism, aviation and private-sector confidence.

    According to recent reports, earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump noted that renewed attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" if negotiations produce a "very strong agreement." However, on Monday, Trump threatened that Tehran could face fresh U.S. strikes next year if the two countries failed to strike a deal, as per Fox News.

    "We can we cannot promise the world for any storms that will land on our shore, but we can always promise that the UAE's economy is ready for any storm," Al Marri said.

    He added that next year the UAE's economy will have a "different" model than the one before the conflict and investments will be focused on building factories and "things that we really need in times of crisis.".

    The World Bank in October stated it expects the UAE's economy to recover next year, driven by rising oil production and exports and a rebound in tourism, trade, transportation, financial services, and construction.

    It warned that the improvement in economic activity in the UAE largely depends on the duration and intensity of the Iran war, with a faster de-escalation likely to accelerate the recovery in services exports and private-sector activity.

    Industry News: Prediction markets outlook for stocks in 2026 dims amid AI sell-off

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off, prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.
    • It has been revealed that on platform Kalshi, speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026.
    • Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off, prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.

    It has been revealed that on platform Kalshi, speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%.

    Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices.

    On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too.

    The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%.

    The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.

    "The market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out," the note said.

    The Stock Trader's Almanac sees 2026 following the year-end pattern of 2018, when the Federal Reserve was in a tightening cycle in a midterm year. The Fed is widely expected to hike rates at its December meeting.

    In a recent development, in that scenario, the Stock Trader's Almanac thinks more churn is to come. "The low is more likely in mid- to late December than this week.".

    Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

    #131879. Industry News: U.S. proposes latest tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (632 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: U.S. proposes latest tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (632 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the U.S.
    • Recent findings suggest that the administration released those and other trade investigations in March, weeks after the Supreme Court unraveled a major piece of President Donald Trump's tariff-heavy economic policy by striking down his "liberation day" duties.
    • The latest action targets foreign economies that create, sustain or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors that the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the U.S. is preparing latest tariffs on 14 economies, including China, the EU, Japan and India, following investigations into what the Trump administration says are excess manufacturing practices that disadvantage U.S. commerce.

    Recent findings suggest that the administration released those and other trade investigations in March, weeks after the Supreme Court unraveled a major piece of President Donald Trump's tariff-heavy economic policy by striking down his "liberation day" duties. Trump has since been accused by critics of his tariffs of trying to revive the canceled duties using other legal authorities.

    The latest action targets foreign economies that create, sustain or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors that the U.S. finds unreasonable and burdensome or restrictive to its commerce, a senior U.S. official told reporters Tuesday evening.

    The upcoming tariffs are "targeted," not blanket rates, and will vary for each economy, and many will not exceed the rates established in previously reached trade deals, stated the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the forthcoming duties.

    The rates, which mostly range from 15% to 20%, are "not really additive" and generally will not stack on top of existing duties, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Wednesday morning.

    "In effect, it'll look more like a top up," Greer noted. "When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points.".

    An exception is China, which faces a 20% rate under the upcoming tariff policy, "so it will go up some," Greer stated. But at the same time, both countries are moving to remove tariffs on some of each other's goods in what Greer called "stability-generating activity through this action.".

    The senior U.S. official mentioned Tuesday that the 20% rate will come on top of the so-called forced technology transfer-related tariffs of roughly 25%, which were implemented during Trump's first presidential term. U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods will therefore reach about 45%, give or take for different goods, the official said.

    Average U.S. tariffs rates on Chinese goods stood at about 36.5% as of July, according to the Congressional Research Service.

    Greer also noted on CNBC that the new policy likely will not take effect for months.

    "We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing," he said. "I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don't think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now.".

    It has been revealed that the administration indicates the tariffs target what it calls "overcapacity" — excess industrial production, often supported by government subsidies, that allows cheaper goods to flood global markets and undercut U.S. producers.

    China has disputed the allegations. "The so-called 'overcapacity' does not really exist," China's foreign ministry said Wednesday before the official reports were released by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, according to Reuters.

    The overcapacity levies are being imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The Trump administration invoked the same statute to launch investigations into 60 economies over alleged forced-labor issues.

    Those investigations, which also began in March, led to broad tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from dozens of countries covering 99.4% of U.S. imports.

    The Section 301 actions came weeks after the Supreme Court struck down the near-global tariffs that Trump had enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

    In a recent development, shortly after the court's ruling, Trump invoked Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose a 10% global tariff. That tariff expired after 150 days, and was immediately replaced with the forced-labor-related duties.

    An ongoing lawsuit accuses the Trump administration of citing forced-labor problems as a "pretext" in pursuit of reviving Trump's worldwide tariff regime.

    #131875. Taking on Starlink: Europe’s largest satellite factory opens in push to rival Musk

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (437 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Taking on Starlink: Europe’s largest satellite factory opens in push to rival Musk

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (437 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The largest satellite factory in Europe was inaugurated in Belgium this week, boosting the continent's efforts to challenge Elon Musk's Starlink and reduce reliance on U.S.
    • Privately held Belgian satellite manufacturer Aerospacelab secured a 2.4-billion-euro ($2.6 billion) contract in September to manufacture 264 of the 348 satellites planned for IRIS², the European Union's answer to SpaceX's Starlink business.
    • Aerospacelab said this will "form the backbone of Europe's sovereign, secure, and resilient connectivity infrastructure by 2030." It will be named Ectro from Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The largest satellite factory in Europe was inaugurated in Belgium this week, boosting the continent's efforts to challenge Elon Musk's Starlink and reduce reliance on U.S. space infrastructure.

    Privately held Belgian satellite manufacturer Aerospacelab secured a 2.4-billion-euro ($2.6 billion) contract in September to manufacture 264 of the 348 satellites planned for IRIS², the European Union's answer to SpaceX's Starlink business.

    Aerospacelab said this will "form the backbone of Europe's sovereign, secure, and resilient connectivity infrastructure by 2030." It will be named Ectro from Nov. 30.

    Its new oval-shaped, 20,000-square-meter facility in southern Belgium, inaugurated by Belgian King Philippe, will be able to produce up to 500 satellites annually, which would make it the world's third-largest satellite production site, according to the Belgian royal palace.

    Employees are expected to move into the megafactory in January, and production is slated to begin by the end of 2028, according to AFP.

    Satellite connectivity has become increasingly key to everyday life as well as national security.

    It provides internet access to remote locations and defense equipment like warships and fighter jets, and lets governments and militaries communicate securely where Earth-based networks are unavailable or disrupted.

    It has been revealed that the importance of such capabilities has become particularly apparent in Ukraine, as the country's military relies heavily on Starlink connectivity to fight Russian forces. Recent restrictions to the service over Russian-occupied territory reported by Ukrainian officials further underscored the way geopolitical conflict may depend on commercial businesses.

    But Europe still has a long way to go in challenging Starlink's dominance.

    SpaceX says it has more than 11,000 Starlink satellites in low Earth orbit, making it by far the largest satellite constellation in the world, and intends up to 100,000 satellites.

    Among the challengers is Amazon, whose satellite business, Amazon Leo, has deployed over 400 satellites and prepares an initial in-orbit constellation of more than 3,200.

    Meanwhile, French Eutelsat operates more than 600 satellites in low Earth orbit through its OneWeb constellation. The company is also part of the SpaceRISE consortium alongside SES and Hispasat, tasked with developing and operating IRIS².

    The European Commission has called IRIS² a "strategic asset to achieve space sovereignty in the face of commercial satellite constellations, such as Starlink." The aim is for first debuts to take place by the end of 2029, with initial services expected soon after.

    In August, the Commission and SpaceRISE consortium announced they were expanding the main constellation from 282 to 348 satellites, increasing its secure communications capacity for EU governments by 60%.

    Defense and security applications were the main drivers of the expanded scope, the Commission mentioned.

    It has been revealed that I asked Claude after Friday's close what I should do about the tanking stock market. Its advice was surprisingly useful: avoid panic selling and look for opportunities. A 40 VIX, which it touched Friday, might provide those opportunities. Specifically, a higher VIX (higher options premiums) signals fear, but it also creates an opportunity to sell elevated premium in some premium stocks, like Amazon.

    According to recent reports, amazon's cloud business is growing at its fastest pace in nearly five years. AWS revenue rose 39.3% YoY in the third quarter, and management reported a $578 billion backlog. Trailing 12-month operating cash flow rose 29% to $168.3 billion. However, infrastructure investment accelerated, resulting in more than $42 billion in negative cash flow. The competing forces of accelerating growth and the cost of supplying it could keep the stock in its range over the next four weeks. Its shares are only off 14% from its recent highs, comparatively better than the Nasdaq Composite's near 19% decline.

    AWS demand supports the lower end of the range. The backlog gives Amazon a basis for adding capacity even as investors scrutinize the cash cost. Cash spending could temper an upside rerating.

    The next leg higher may require evidence that new capacity can earn attractive returns at this scale, and that evidence may be in short supply over the next couple of months.

    Sources indicate that sell the Dec. 18, 2026 AMZN 235/285 strangle for an indicative $5.90 credit per share.

    Max reward — $590 per strangle if AMZN finishes between $235 and $285 at expiration, before fees.

    Breakevens at expiration — $229.10 and $290.90.

    In a recent development, max risk — Unlimited on the uncovered call, but one should think of the trade as risking getting short at a net price above $290, a nearly 13% premium to today's closing price. The downside loss would reach $22,910 per strangle if AMZN fell to zero. The credit is roughly 2.3% of a $260 reference share price over four weeks, or nearly 30% on a simple annualized basis. That comparison uses the share price as its denominator. Actual return on capital depends on margin and the cost to close or settle the trade.

    Sources indicate that buying in bear markets, as the Nasdaq just touched, is never easy. But those opportunities don't present themselves too often. What are you going to do with it?

    #131868. Latin America has the copper and energy the AI build-out needs. Infrastructure is the test

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1168 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Latin America has the copper and energy the AI build-out needs. Infrastructure is the test

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Latin America’s copper, energy and mineral resources could play a growing role in supplying the global artificial-intelligence build-out, as data centers and electrification drive demand for power and raw materials.
    • But for investors, it's less about whether Latin America has the resources than whether governments can turn them into viable projects.
    • Recent findings suggest that "We are going through an acceleration in energy demand growth.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Latin America’s copper, energy and mineral resources could play a growing role in supplying the global artificial-intelligence build-out, as data centers and electrification drive demand for power and raw materials.

    But for investors, it's less about whether Latin America has the resources than whether governments can turn them into viable projects.

    Recent findings suggest that "We are going through an acceleration in energy demand growth. We need every possible energy source available," Michele Della Vigna, head of natural resources research for Goldman Sachs, told CNBC. "Ultimately, what drives economic growth is energy," he added.

    In a recent development, ben Kumar, head of strategy for wealth, investment and public policy at 7IM, suggested Latin America could benefit, given the physical materials needed for AI equipment and data centers. "We are currently neutral in the short term, but if the materials and mining cycle continues, we could see this moving to positive in a few months," he stated.

    In a recent development, the investment case varies across the region. Chile has copper; Argentina is expanding oil and gas exports; and Brazil has abundant renewable power and significant rare earth reserves.

    Chile's copper sector illustrates both the supply potential and the constraints to expanding supply. Copper production fell 8.5% in the first nine months of 2026, according to the state copper commission Cochilco, as lower ore grades, maintenance, and operational disruptions constrained supply.

    Recent findings suggest that but demand for refined copper is set to grow 1.6% this year and 2% next year, according to the International Copper Study Group. Supply is struggling to keep pace with demand from expanding electricity grids.

    Recent findings suggest that chile's copper commission has raised its 2027 price forecast to $5.95 a pound, from $5.10. Codelco, the state-owned copper producer, may also have scope to increase supply, including through proposed public-private partnerships.

    Rafael Ch, partner and senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, sees demand continuing to grow. "As countries expand electricity grids, they need more copper regardless of which power source they choose," he said.

    Industry observers note that the scale of the opportunity will depend in part on how quickly energy demand grows. Goldman Sachs forecasts that global power demand for data centers will grow by 170% by 2030. The IEA projected in April that global data center electricity consumption would rise from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030.

    Recent findings suggest that the investment case also depends on whether the region can capture more value from the resources it produces. Latin America and the Caribbean refined only 26% of the copper they mined in 2025, according to the IEA.

    "Cautious optimism is justified and there will be massive critical mineral demand," said Monica de Bolle, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.

    "But improving refining capacity will be crucial to capture more of that value," she added.

    It has been revealed that some projects have already secured financing. Chilean explorer Marimaca Copper Corp selected a preferred lender for a $400 million debt facility to build a mine on Oct. 28. The funding will go towards developing an open-pit mine in the north of Chile that will produce 50,000 metric tons of refined copper annually. Production is expected from 2029.

    Argentina reveals the other side of the opportunity: strong oil and gas resources, but insufficient infrastructure to get more production to global markets.

    "I see an opportunity in the infrastructure that gets Argentine oil and gas to market. A producer in Vaca Muerta can have excellent wells and still struggle to expand exports without pipeline capacity and access to ports.

    That gives investors a reason to look at transport and export infrastructure alongside production," Rafael Ch, partner and senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, added. Vaca Muerta is Argentina's vast shale basin.

    Industry observers note that argentina is also attracting investment in drilling and export infrastructure. International capital markets have reopened to investment in drilling and pipelines in Argentina. That investment has already driven the build-out of a pipeline and port. Argentina will then be able to export far more crude oil. Chevron and American oil tycoon Harold Hamm have also increased their investments in Argentina.

    Brazil's case rests partly on its renewable-heavy power mix. About 89% of the country's electricity was generated from renewable sources in 2025, according to the country's Ministry of Mines and Energy.

    "That puts Brazil in a strong position to benefit as AI and data centers drive up demand," Stephanie Link, chief investment strategist and portfolio manager at Hightower Advisors, told CNBC.

    But while Brazil has the world's second-largest reported rare-earth reserves, its estimated mine production is far smaller than China's. USGS estimates put Brazil's output at 2,000 metric tons in 2025, compared with China's 270,000 metric tons. Brazil's reserves are estimated at 11 million metric tons by the USGS, second only to China's 44 million metric tons.

    For investors, the gap between Brazil's vast reserves and limited current production is both the opportunity and the execution risk.

    For investors, the policy question is whether governments can make projects viable and keep them on track.

    Luis Costa, Citi's global head of emerging markets strategy, noted governments need to offer incentives, particularly in the early stages of projects, because infrastructure lags the region's resource wealth. He also stressed that support must last: infrastructure projects can take several years to develop.

    The World Bank's Latin America and the Caribbean Economic Upgrade for 2026 projects growth for the region of 2.2%, and highlights the "restricted fiscal space, sticky inflation and high borrowing costs.".

    "The economic policy and fiscal policy needs to get in line as markets are globally becoming more sensitive to fiscal stories," stated Costa.

    It has been revealed that brazil will need to establish fiscal credibility to attract investment, particularly if higher public spending puts additional pressure on debt and borrowing costs. "If investors doubt the government can stabilize public debt, companies' long-term financing costs could stay high even as the central bank lowers its policy rate," Ch added.

    Sources indicate that with Argentina set for national elections in October 2027, political continuity will also matter for energy investment. "A return to tighter currency controls or persistent deficits would make companies more likely to delay projects, even in an oil field with attractive economics," said Ch.

    Pro-business President Javier Milei faces a tight race for re-election, though a change in leadership would not necessarily undermine medium- to long-term investment.

    "There is also the possibility of a pragmatic Peronist ticket emerging, which markets would be satisfied with," mentioned Nicolas Jaquier, emerging-market fixed-income portfolio manager at Ninety One.

    For those governing across Latin America, policies to unlock its wealth of resources will be key for it to emerge as a winner from the AI demand boom.

    "Supply chain security is becoming more and more relevant, and if commodities take off Latin America can be a clear and obvious winner," said Kumar.

    Hardware & Chips ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    S&P warns Nvidia credit rating could be cut over 'rising' management and governance risk

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (476 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nvidia's credit rating could be cut by one notch over the next 90 days if the organization continues to have "deficiencies" in its management and governance framework, S&P Global Ratings mentioned in the wake of the Jensen Huang's ouster and reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.
    • "News regarding the CEO and questions regarding potential export control violations have exposed vulnerabilities in Nvidia's management and governance framework, especially in regard to its board structure, composition, and effectiveness," S&P remarked in a Wednesday note.
    • Nvidia currently holds an AA rating, the third-highest level.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nvidia's credit rating could be cut by one notch over the next 90 days if the organization continues to have "deficiencies" in its management and governance framework, S&P Global Ratings mentioned in the wake of the Jensen Huang's ouster and reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.

    "News regarding the CEO and questions regarding potential export control violations have exposed vulnerabilities in Nvidia's management and governance framework, especially in regard to its board structure, composition, and effectiveness," S&P remarked in a Wednesday note.

    Nvidia currently holds an AA rating, the third-highest level.

    S&P has placed the chipmaker on "CreditWatch with negative implications," though any potential downgrade would be limited to one notch, to AA-, unless investigations or disclosures lead the agency to conclude that Nvidia's reputation or future prospects have also been harmed.

    A downgrade can pressure bond prices, push yields higher and raise borrowing costs. Nvidia priced $25 billion of investment-grade senior notes in June, with maturities from 2028 through 2056, shortly after S&P upgraded the firm from AA- to AA.

    Nvidia has about $32.5 billion of bonds in the U.S. high-grade corporate bond index, according to Bloomberg.

    It has been revealed that S&P's Wednesday note follows Moody's Ratings changing its outlook on Nvidia to stable from positive on Nov. 18, citing governance concerns, and leaving that outlook unchanged after Huang's return on Monday.

    In its note, S&P cited the "long tenure" of certain board members as a reason their independence may be "compromised" and said Nvidia's management and governance risk was "rising.".

    The ratings agency added that it remained unaware of any remedial action taken by the board to address what could be "meaningful" management and governance deficiencies.

    Recent findings suggest that chairman Harvey Jones and early investor Tench Coxe have served on Nvidia's board since 1993, while Brooke Seawell joined in 1997. Mark Stevens served from 1993 to 2006 and rejoined the board in 2008.

    S&P also flagged questions around geopolitical risk management and internal controls arising from Nvidia's exposure to China.

    "While Nvidia management has delivered significant returns for its stakeholders over decades, weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning have brought questions around the "key man" risk to the forefront," S&P's Andrew Chang and David Tsui stated.

    Chang and Tsui noted that Huang's resignation and subsequent reinstatement did not resolve questions about the board's oversight of executive conduct.

    The agency also intends to meet with Nvidia's board and management to discuss prepares to address those deficiencies, particularly around "board independence, effective management oversight and a credible leadership succession strategy.".

    Industry observers note that huang returned less than two weeks after Jones said Nvidia's directors did not intend to reinstate him. The board later voted unanimously to bring Huang back, sending Nvidia shares up as much as 36% during Monday's session.

    Nvidia shares are down about 12.5% since Monday's close.

    • Industry observers note that goldman Sachs Alternatives' inaugural survey of high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth investors found 47% of European respondents saw alternatives as the best way to gain exposure to AI and future tech growth, compared to just 24% of U.S.
    • The survey found a significant gap between the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Wealthy Europeans are looking to alternative asset classes to build exposure to artificial intelligence themes amid turbulence in public markets.

    Industry observers note that goldman Sachs Alternatives' inaugural survey of high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth investors found 47% of European respondents saw alternatives as the best way to gain exposure to AI and future tech growth, compared to just 24% of U.S. investors.

    The survey found a significant gap between the U.S. and Europe in terms of investor knowledge of alternatives, which include assets like private equity, property and infrastructure. Goldman remarked 82% of European respondents are familiar with the alternative investments market — compared to 50% of U.S. investors.

    It has been revealed that goldman polled 1,000 investors with at least 1 million in investable assets in their local currency across the U.K., France, Germany, Italy and Switzerland. The survey was carried out between June 29 and Aug. 18 this year.

    The report on the findings, published Wednesday, did not specify the proportion of respondents who already have a stake in some kind of alternative investment — but wealthy Europeans appeared particularly bullish on the space.

    According to recent reports, private equity made up the largest proportion of current alternatives holdings. Among wealthy Europeans with alternatives exposure, 62% said they invested in private equity. The second most commonly held asset class was private real estate, which was backed by 51% of European alternatives investors. Hedge funds were held by 37% of European alternatives owners, and private infrastructure was held by 30%.

    Industry observers note that one in four respondents who did not already own an alternative investment remarked they were likely to invest in the market in the coming 12 months. Among those already in the space, 26% said they were likely to increase their allocations over the next year, while just 5% said they planned to decrease their exposure.

    Of the European investors who already owned alternatives, 54% remarked their assets had performed as expected, while 44% said their assets had exceeded their expectations to the upside. Only 2% said their alternative investments had performed worse than expected.

    "Recent reforms gave individual investors unprecedented access to alternative asset classes like private equity, venture capital, and private credit," Kyle Kniffen, global head of alternatives for third-party wealth at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said in Wednesday's report.

    He added that wealthy investors "look ready to jump at the opportunity.".

    "Our survey indicates satisfaction among current alts owners is high and adoption looks set to increase," Kniffen said.

    Alternative investments have increasingly become a staple of high-net-worth individuals' investment portfolios.

    Over the past year, JPMorgan Asset Management's private wealth alternative assets in the Asia-Pacific region have jumped 40%, while BNY Wealth indicates alternative investments now account for 60% of single-family office portfolios — recently surpassing traditional assets for the first time.

    But investing in alternatives carries risks. Private equity, for example, can lock up capital for long periods, and although the number of exits ticked slightly higher last year, the value of those deals fell.

    Industry observers note that concerns about private credit, meanwhile, have dominated headlines, with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warning on Oct. 14, 2025, that "cockroaches" were likely to be lurking in private markets.

    — CNBC's Lee Ying Shan contributed to this article.

    #131853. U.S. tariff-hike threats pile pressure on partners to sign trade deals

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1553 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    U.S. tariff-hike threats pile pressure on partners to sign trade deals

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Trump administration has unveiled a fresh tariff salvo on more than a dozen trading partners, with China, Vietnam, and India facing some of the steepest potential rates and mounting pressure to conclude trade deals with Washington.
    • The proposed tariffs, framed as curbing excess industrial capacity, start at 15% for the European Union, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan and rise to as much as 35% for Vietnam.
    • Trade Representative's Office remarked it intends to cap the upcoming duties at lower levels for countries that have completed trade deals or are still negotiating with Washington.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Trump administration has unveiled a fresh tariff salvo on more than a dozen trading partners, with China, Vietnam, and India facing some of the steepest potential rates and mounting pressure to conclude trade deals with Washington.

    The proposed tariffs, framed as curbing excess industrial capacity, start at 15% for the European Union, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan and rise to as much as 35% for Vietnam.

    The U.S. Trade Representative's Office remarked it intends to cap the upcoming duties at lower levels for countries that have completed trade deals or are still negotiating with Washington.

    Sources indicate that the overall impact on the region is likely to be limited, said Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics. The proposal "puts most of the targeted countries back where they were earlier in the year," he said, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's emergency tariffs in February.

    Still, the proposal could give some countries an incentive to speed up trade talks in order to lock in lower tariff rates, analysts said.

    On Wednesday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the latest policy likely will not take effect for months, with a senior U.S. official saying the duties could take effect as early as January.

    China faces a capped rate of 20%, on top of an existing 25% tariff imposed during President Donald Trump's first term. The rate could rise to 40% if the trade truce reached in South Korea last October is not extended beyond January, the USTR remarked.

    Beijing has rejected Washington's claim of excess capacity while vowing to take measures necessary to protect its rights.

    On Thursday, Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong called on Washington to "rectify its wrongdoing and return to the right track of resolving complications through dialogue.".

    In a recent development, he was responding to Washington's plan to raise tariffs following its Section 301 investigations, while the ministry also urged the U.S. to implement $30 billion of reciprocal tariff cuts agreed by the two sides in late September.

    The renewed tensions come despite several conciliatory meetings between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping this year, as well as what Williams described as Trump's "apparent lack of concern" about allegations that Chinese technology firms have circumvented U.S. chip export controls.

    The two leaders are expected to meet for a fourth time this year at the Group of 20 leaders summit in Miami in December.

    "While not happy, Beijing seems prepared to live with the fresh rates provided that they don't exceed 20%," remarked Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

    By retaining the option to raise levies if bilateral talks deteriorate, Washington is using the tariffs as leverage to "secure expected shipments of critical minerals and rare earths, and further purchases of U.S. agricultural goods," Cutler remarked.

    Recent findings suggest that washington has warned that tariffs on Chinese goods could double to 40% if the USTR finds that Beijing is not engaging. "If the trade war did start up again, today's measures provide the U.S. with some ammunition," Williams mentioned.

    Even the sweeping actions against the other 13 trading partners appear aimed squarely at China, noted Williams, who tallied that the word "China" appears 253 times in the USTR's report on Vietnam, and 315 times in the document on the European Union.

    "Foremost among the 'unreasonable acts, policies, and practices' that these countries are criticised for is being slow to restrict imports and FDI from China," Williams said.

    While the proposed tariffs generally lift average rates only modestly, India and Vietnam stand out because of the wider gaps between the rates they would face with and without a deal, analysts remarked.

    India and Vietnam face proposed tariffs of 25% and 35%, respectively, but those rates could fall sharply to 17% and 20% if ongoing talks with the U.S. produce reciprocal trade agreements.

    The two countries have "a strong incentive" to conclude deals with Washington to secure the lower rates, Cutler said.

    Vietnam's trade ministry noted Thursday that it was working with the U.S. to complete a trade deal as soon as possible, according to Reuters. India could also gain an edge over some Asian rivals through comparatively lower levies if Latest Delhi concludes its long-pending trade deal with Washington.

    Singapore faces a similar challenge. The proposal sets a maximum potential rate of 20% on its exports, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, which could fall to 10% if it reaches an agreement on reciprocal trade with the U.S. or concludes other negotiations addressing the USTR's findings, according to Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry.

    The ministry noted it disagreed with the findings and was "very disappointed" with the proposed action, arguing that it failed to account for the structure of Singapore's economy.

    Speaking to reporters, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said that about 33%, or 9.4 billion Singapore dollars ($7.2 billion) of direct exports will be affected, and the effective tariff rate on affected Singapore exports will rise to 10.3% from the current 7.8%, should Washington impose the highest levy of 20%. "I'm also very surprised that this has happened because this is not something that you would expect from an notable major trading partner," Gan added, saying "We have been working together for many years, and we have an FTA with the U.S.," Gan said, referring to the U.S.-Singapore Free Trade Agreement that was in force since 2004.

    Industry observers note that under the FTA, Singapore imposes zero tariffs on U.S. goods, while the U.S. has run a trade surplus with the city-state for more than 20 years, the ministry mentioned. That surplus grew to $33 billion in 2025 from $27 billion in 2024.

    Singapore remarked it would submit further comments during the public consultation period and urge the USTR to reconsider.

    Exemptions for semiconductors and other electronics should cushion the impact on South Korea and Taiwan, whose economies are heavily concentrated in those sectors, analysts noted.

    The USTR singled out South Korea for its concentration in memory-chip production and what it described as outsized government support. Yet it excluded the country's chips from the proposed excess-capacity tariffs.

    Sources indicate that taiwan, which faces an excess-capacity tariff cap of 15%, also benefits from exemptions for other electronics, including mobile phones and networking equipment. Its effective tariff rate would rise to about 9% from 6%, Williams estimated.

    Switzerland was hit with a shock 39% tariff rate back in 2025, targeting significant exports, from chemicals and pharmaceuticals to gold, watches and chocolates. In November 2025, it negotiated a deal that slashed U.S. duties to 15% in return for a commitment to invest billions and increase manufacturing Stateside.

    According to recent reports, in March 2026, the U.S. introduced further Section 301 investigations into Switzerland over "unfair or discriminatory trade practices," landing on a recommendation to impose an additional 15% tariff.

    Industry observers note that switzerland's Economy Ministry told CNBC that the country rejected the allegations raised during the investigations and noted it had already presented its arguments during bilateral consultations with the U.S. Treasury.

    Industry observers note that the ministry added that it assumed the latest recommendation was consistent with the deal struck in November 2025 and said it was in close contact with U.S. authorities as it reviews next steps.

    Officials for both Switzerland and the European Union stated during trade discussions last year that while they had a trade surplus with Washington in goods, the relationship was balanced when accounting for both trade and services, where the U.S. dominates in areas such as technology and finance.

    It has been revealed that brussels said it was assessing the U.S. report but rejected its finding that Europe was a source of industrial overcapacity.

    "To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity," European Commission Spokesperson Olof Gill mentioned in a statement.

    Industry observers note that "The EU and the U.S. share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action," Gill remarked.

    The EU expects any measure taken from the investigation to respect the existing joint agreement of a 15% all-inclusive ceiling on EU goods, Gill added.

    Sources indicate that EU trade ministers are due to speak with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Monday.

    Citi analysts noted they expected a hit on European retailers if the measures stay as confirmed, with the likes of Adidas, H&M, Puma and Primark potentially seeing downgrades on full-year 2027 earnings.

    In a recent development, inga Fechner, senior economist for global trade at ING, said in a Wednesday note that the U.S. "tariff wall keeps changing, but it isn't coming down," adding that "U.S. protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind.".

    While the newly Democrat-controlled Congress could try to restrict presidential tariff authority, remove individual duties or apply greater scrutiny via hearings and investigations, actually reversing the measures will be difficult while Trump retains veto power, she said.

    "We don't think the blue wave will mark a return to free trade. The Biden years already showed that tariffs in strategically crucial sectors enjoy support across political camps.".

    Protectionist moves become more targeted, she added, adding to a complex system of country- and sector-specific duties based on different legal authorities.

    — CNBC's Evelyn Cheng contributed to this report.

    • Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, investors often favor dividend stocks for their regular income and the promise of potential share price appreciation. But selecting the right dividend stocks from a huge pool of companies can be difficult.

    Top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend-paying stocks, as their recommendations are backed by thorough analysis of a company's financials.

    Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

    Devon Energy (DVN), an independent oil and natural gas exploration and production company, reported better-than-expected third-quarter results. The company unveiled a quarterly dividend of 32 cents per share for the fourth quarter, payable December 30. Based on the fixed dividends paid over the trailing 12 months, DVN yields 2.85%.

    According to recent reports, after hosting a virtual investor meeting with management, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Devon, with a price target of $59. Mehta said that he is now more confident in management's outlook for delivering strong near-term capital returns as well as efforts to drive operational efficiencies and productivity gains.

    Devon sees an opportunity to increase share repurchases, driven by solid free cash flow (FCF), contributions from the Eagle Ford divestiture and continued improvement in the balance sheet, Mehta noted. Devon expects share buybacks worth more than $1 billion in Q4 2026, up from $414 million in the third quarter, backed by a strong pricing backdrop and improved capital efficiency.

    Sources indicate that mehta, a 5-star analyst, said Devon expects about $6.3 billion of excess FCF in 2027, including about $3.5 billion of net proceeds from the Eagle Ford sale. That would enable the tech giant to accelerate buybacks while progressing toward its goal of reducing gross debt to about $9 billion by early 2027. Mehta noted that under DVN's framework to return up to 70% of annual FCF, management favors share buybacks as it believes the stock is discounted compared to large-cap peers.

    "Management expects continued capital efficiency gains from merger synergies, extended laterals, surfactant adoption and development of the newly acquired federal acreage," Mehta said.

    It has been revealed that mehta ranks No. 876 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 8.1%. See Devon Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

    It has been revealed that energy Transfer (ET), is a limited partnership that operates about 140,000 miles of pipeline and associated energy infrastructure. The company recently announced third-quarter results showing net income per common unit growing about 18% year-over-year, to 33 cents. ET's cash distribution for Q3 2026 was 34.25 cents per common unit, up more than 3% year-over-year. At an annualized distribution of $1.37 per share, Energy Transfer yields more than 7%.

    TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Energy Transfer with a price target of $25. The company delivered better-than-expected Q3 results and unveiled the 1.2 billion cubic feet per day (bcf/d) South Mississippi Pipeline, a 215-mile, 36-inch natural gas line linking the Perryville Hub to the Florida Gas Transmission (FGT) network, Gabelman said. The project is supported by 20-year firm transportation agreements and is expected to enter service in 2030. ET expects to ultimately own 51% of the $1.6 billion project.

    Industry observers note that the 5-star analyst mentioned that Energy Transfer lowered its 2026 capital spending outlook to $5.5 billion (midpoint of the guidance range) from $5.75 billion due to project timing. Energy Transfer expects capex to rise to $7 billion in 2027, while Gabelman projects $5 billion in both 2028 and 2029, based on disclosed projects.

    Sources indicate that gabelman also highlighted management's commentary about optimization initiatives contributing an incremental $800 million to 2026 earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, a larger benefit than in recent years. "A return to less commodity volatility should the [Middle East] war end could bring some relative downside, though this is offset by continued strong growth prospects," he noted.

    Gabelman ranks No. 397 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15.4%. See Energy Transfer KPIs on TipRanks.

    Oil and gas exploration and production firm ConocoPhillips (COP) delivered better-than-expected Q3 performance. The company confirmed an 11% hike in its quarterly dividend to 93 cents per share, effective with the Q4 dividend payable on December 1. Based on the dividends paid over the trailing 12 months, COP yields about 2.6%.

    Following the Q3 results, Wells Fargo analyst Sam Margolin repeated a buy rating on ConocoPhillips, citing strong potential for further dividend increases. Margolin also trimmed his price target to $185 from $189 to reflect timing effects and the WAHA forward curve, though he said that COP could still re-rate as its natural portfolio lifecycle provides stronger protection against inflationary pressures than peers. The Waha forward curve tracks future natural gas prices based on the West Texas Waha hub.

    Sources indicate that margolin, another 5-star analyst, highlighted that ConocoPhillips' Q3 2026 adjusted earnings per share of $3.27 was well above Wells Fargo and the Street's estimates of $3.04 and $3.05, respectively. Earnings were driven by solid price realizations, partially offset by higher depletion, depreciation and amortization and purchased commodities.

    Margolin also noted COP's dividend increase and said the accelerated buyback enabled by current commodity prices could further support long-term dividend growth. He sees the possibility of ConocoPhillips' dividend growth rate exceeding its current 6% cost of equity into the end of the decade. Margolin expects COP to sustain an 8% dividend compound annual growth rate through 2029 while repurchasing $6.4 billion of stock annually, and reducing net debt-to-capital to less than 9% by the end of 2028 based on the assumption of an average Brent crude oil price of $75 a barrel.

    "The message on the 3Q call was similar to that of 2Q, reiterating the moderation in reinvestment rate and commitment to dividend growth through the Willow start-up and after," Margolin remarked.

    According to recent reports, margolin ranks No. 189 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 69% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.6%. See ConocoPhillips Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

    Norse Atlantic suspends all flights, warns it may file for bankruptcy after share price collapse

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Norse Atlantic suspended all of its flights on Thursday and warned it may have to file for bankruptcy after its stock collapsed on Wednesday following its warning about its "critical" financial situation.
    • Oslo-listed shares of Norse closed 85% lower on Wednesday.
    • In a recent development, "The board of directors continues to consider options to secure short-term financing," Norse remarked in a Thursday statement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Norse Atlantic suspended all of its flights on Thursday and warned it may have to file for bankruptcy after its stock collapsed on Wednesday following its warning about its "critical" financial situation.

    Oslo-listed shares of Norse closed 85% lower on Wednesday.

    In a recent development, "The board of directors continues to consider options to secure short-term financing," Norse remarked in a Thursday statement. "If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board's intention to file for bankruptcy.".

    The airline added that "there can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found.".

    Checks by CNBC showed the airline was still selling tickets for flights on Friday and beyond as of 9 a.m. Oslo time on Thursday.

    Warning signs first popped up when PK786 from London to Islamabad and PK710 from Manchester to Lahore were cancelled because of "an unexpected operational suspension," the Pakistani flag carrier said on X.

    The airline had been set to operate two Pakistan International Airlines flights Wednesday under a wet-lease agreement, in which one airline provides the aircraft and crew to another. The agreement had only been signed in early October.

    PIA remarked it would operate the routes using its own Boeing 777 aircraft from the next day.

    Norse's own flight Z0 783 from London Gatwick to Orlando was also shown as canceled Wednesday on live air traffic website Flightradar24. London Gatwick's website listed the flight's status for Thursday as "enquire airline.".

    In a bid to stave off financial troubles, Norse cut 75 jobs in May as part of an effort to reduce costs by $50 million, after Eivind Roald replaced founder Bjorn Tore Larsen as CEO in November last year.

    The Norwegian carrier said Wednesday that its situation depended on securing financing for short-term liquidity needs and that it was in discussions about a potential strategic takeover.

    "Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution," the airline mentioned.

    The Norwegian carrier has come under strain due to soaring jet fuel costs since the onset of the Iran war.

    India's largest airline, low-cost carrier IndiGo, entered an agreement with Norse Atlantic in early 2025 to lease six 787-9 aircraft as it introduced flights to Europe and Britain ahead of the arrival of its own widebody planes.

    The agreement concluded at the end of October this year, with IndiGo citing airspace constraints, elevated fuel costs and currency pressures.

    At its peak in 2024, Norse Atlantic had 4,822 scheduled flights. That number dipped to 4,695 in 2025 and 2,565 in 2026, according to aviation analytics company Cirium. The airline had 122 flights scheduled for November this year.

    Industry observers note that norse Atlantic CEO Roald told CNBC in May that he was not "overly concerned" about access to fuel and noted the airline had no indication at the time that the crisis would have an immediate impact. The airline said in October that it was continuing to operate at reduced capacity because of "prolonged high fuel prices.".

    Correction: This story was updated to reflect that Norse shares closed 85% lower on Wednesday.

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Nvidia sellers seek new buyers as U.S. curbs China AI chip access, sources tell CNBC

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (504 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
    • Industry observers note that companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since latest measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov.
    • Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the fresh rule.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.

    Industry observers note that companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since latest measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people stated.

    Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the fresh rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.

    The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.

    It has been revealed that the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, declared an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.

    Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was unveiled, mentioned Duhamel and one of the people.

    Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

    Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.

    The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.

    In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI, of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the manufacturer had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.

    U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes.".

    "For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he remarked.

    "Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries.".

    Recent findings suggest that during Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress remarked the firm was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.
